drapeaux.note: Titres de Griaule traduits littéralement entre parenthèses (Dieu d'eau, Un système soudanais de Sirius, Le Renard pâle) ; les éditions anglaises publiées peuvent porter d'autres titres.

titre: A Star No One Could See
accroche: In 1950, ethnologists publish that the Dogon know of a star invisible to the naked eye. Since then, the origin of this knowledge has been debated.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1931, the French ethnologist Marcel Griaule begins a series of fieldwork missions among the Dogon, in Mali: in 1931, 1935, 1937, and 1938, then every year from 1946 to 1956. At the end of 1946, according to Imbo (1998), he talks for thirty-three consecutive days with Ogotemmêli, a blind Dogon sage, who is said to have learned these things from his father and grandfather, through more than twenty years of oral instruction. These conversations become, in 1948, Dieu d'eau (“God of Water”).

## A star you cannot see with the naked eye

The Sirius system is reported elsewhere: Griaule and his collaborator Germaine Dieterlen describe it in a 1950 article, “Un système soudanais de Sirius” (“A Sudanese Sirius System”), then in Le Renard pâle (“The Pale Fox,” 1965). They report there, along with other elements of Dogon cosmology, a system of stars around Sirius: an invisible companion with an orbital cycle of fifty years. The detail is intriguing, because it matches what astronomers call Sirius B, a white dwarf first observed on January 31, 1862, and whose orbit was determined precisely by photographic techniques only with Lindenblad, in 1970: nothing visible to the naked eye. In this article, Griaule and Dieterlen write that the question of how men without instruments could have known the movements of almost invisible stars has been neither settled nor even raised. The article, translated into English in 1976, then appears in Robert Temple's The Sirius Mystery, long after Griaule's death in 1956.

## Fieldwork that does not find what was left there

In 1991, the Dutch anthropologist Walter van Beek publishes in Current Anthropology “Dogon Restudied,” the findings of a new field investigation among the Dogon. His informants, he reports, do not agree at all among themselves about the star designated by the Sigui festival: one of them sees Venus in it. Only one point unites them: all say they heard about it from Griaule himself. Geneviève Calame-Griaule replies to him in the same journal: she faults him for not having followed the proper steps to acquire the knowledge, and suggests that his informants believed him to be sent by the political and administrative authorities to test the Dogon's Muslim orthodoxy.

## A question that goes beyond anthropology

The puzzle is not limited to Griaule's method: it also touches astronomy. In 1995, Daniel Benest and Jean-Louis Duvent suggest the possible existence of a second companion of Sirius, with an orbital period of six years. In 2008, the astronomers Bonnet-Bidaud and Pantin, using infrared imaging, conclude that the probability of a triple system is now low, though they cannot rule it out entirely: the central region, within 5 astronomical units, remains out of reach. The debate thus concerns the field more than the sky: where did van Beek's informants say they got this star from?

repere.texte: In Current Anthropology, Walter van Beek reports in 1991 that his Dogon informants do not agree among themselves about the star in question, but all agree that they learned of its existence from Griaule.
repere.source: Walter E. A. van Beek, “Dogon Restudied: A Field Evaluation of the Work of Marcel Griaule”, Current Anthropology, vol. 32, no. 2, 1991, pp. 139-167 (including comments and replies)

carte.punch: Griaule said the Dogon knew an invisible star, learned, by their account, from him.
carte.idee: In 1950, Griaule and Dieterlen report that the Dogon know of an invisible companion of Sirius, seen by astronomers in 1862. In 1991, a counter-investigation finds informants who disagree about the star, but are unanimous: they heard of it from Griaule.

quiz.question: What does the field counter-investigation carried out by Walter van Beek among the Dogon in 1991 reveal?
choix: That his informants disagree about the star, but all say they learned of it from Griaule
That the Dogon had actually observed Sirius B through a telescope as early as the 19th century
That the Dogon people never existed as Griaule described them
That Geneviève Calame-Griaule accepted all of van Beek's conclusions
quiz.explication: Van Beek reports complete disagreement among his informants about the star designated by the Sigui festival, but agreement on the origin of what they know about it: Griaule himself. The other answers are wrong: nothing in the sources says the Dogon observed Sirius B through a telescope, or that their people never existed, and Calame-Griaule, on the contrary, challenged van Beek's method in the same journal.

quiz_supplementaire.question: For how many consecutive days did Griaule converse with Ogotemmêli at the end of 1946, according to Imbo (1998)?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: According to Imbo (1998), Griaule spent 33 consecutive days in conversation with the blind Dogon sage Ogotemmêli at the end of 1946; these talks produced Dieu d'eau, published in 1948. The other durations offered do not match this figure.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What have later astronomical studies shown about a possible second companion of Sirius, beyond Sirius B?
choix: That such a companion certainly exists, with an orbital period of six years
That a 1995 study proposes a candidate, judged unlikely by a 2008 study without being ruled out
That Sirius B itself has never been confirmed by astronomers
That the question was definitively closed as early as the 1930s
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Benest and Duvent (1995) suggested a possible companion with a six-year orbital period; Bonnet-Bidaud and Pantin (2008) judge the probability of a triple system now low, without ruling it out entirely. Sirius B, for its part, was first observed in 1862, and its orbit determined by photographic techniques in 1970 (Lindenblad).
